name: Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda; the Mādhva sampradāya)
alt_names: Brahma-sampradāya (its place in the later scheme of four Vaiṣṇava sampradāyas)

tradition.text: the tradition traces the teaching to Nārāyaṇa (as Haṃsa) through Brahmā and a line of teachers; Vyāsa (an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa) fixed it in the Brahmasūtras; in the Kali age Madhva, the third avatāra of Vāyu, re-proclaimed it

scholarly.text: founded by Madhva in the 13th c. CE; living

transmissions_received.what: the Brahmasūtras as the root text, commented on by Madhva
ten principal Upaniṣads, read as teaching difference and Viṣṇu's supremacy
the Pañcarātra accepted as valid scripture (sadāgama); mantra and worship lore
the Mahābhārata and the Gītā as scripture of the highest rank
Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas insofar as they agree with the sadāgamas
authorless Veda, intrinsic validity, the marks of purport (upakrama etc.) — adapted
debate theory and logical vocabulary — adopted in part and criticized

transmissions_given.what: Dvaita doctrine (Hari's supremacy, gradation of souls) sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas, several of them disciples of Mādhva ascetics (Śrīpādarāja, Vyāsatīrtha, Vādirāja)
the Gauḍīya tradition claims descent from Madhva's line through Mādhavendra Purī; the claim is disputed (see brw:dvaita-gaudiya-parampara)

distinctive_positions: Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa, Hari) alone is independent (svatantra); Lakṣmī, all souls, matter, time and the Veda are dependent (paratantra) on him (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 1; Tattvaviveka 1).
Five real and eternal differences (pañca-bheda) — God–soul, God–matter, soul–soul, soul–matter, matter–matter — hold in every state, including liberation (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 1.68–71).
The world is real (satya); the Advaita doctrines of māyā, the world's falsity (mithyātva) and the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) are refuted (the ten prakaraṇas; Nyāyāmṛta).

Souls are innately graded (tāratamya) and fall into three classes — fit for liberation (mukti-yogya), ever-transmigrating (nitya-saṃsārin), fit for blinding darkness (tamo-yogya); a soul's fitness is beginningless and unalterable (Tattvasaṅkhyāna 4–7; MBTN 1.86–95).
Liberation is the soul's enjoyment of its own intrinsic bliss, graded even among the liberated (ānanda-tāratamya), in eternal difference from and dependence on Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu is full of infinite auspicious qualities and free of every defect; 'nirguṇa' means free of prakṛti's qualities; his qualities, acts, forms and avatāras are not different from him (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 3).
Without Nārāyaṇa's grace there is no liberation, and without knowledge there is no abundant grace (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 1.1.1).
Bhakti is firm love for Viṣṇu exceeding all other love, preceded by knowledge of his greatness (MBTN 1.85); it continues in liberation as eternal bliss (MBTN 1.104).

Three means of valid knowledge — perception, inference, authoritative word; perception is sevenfold, the witness (sākṣin) plus six senses; what the sākṣin establishes is never sublated (Pramāṇalakṣaṇa; Anuvyākhyāna).
Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa) is the highest of souls; grace descends through the higher beings; Madhva is Vāyu's third avatāra after Hanumān and Bhīma (MBTN 32.162–166).
God is the efficient cause of the world, not its material cause; prakṛti is the material cause.

All words, letters and scriptures in their primary sense designate Viṣṇu; the Veda is authorless; valid scripture (sadāgama) is the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pañcarātra, the original Rāmāyaṇa and the Purāṇas that agree with them (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
The soul is a reflection (pratibimba) of God — dependent on and similar to its original (bimba), and eternally distinct from it.
Chāndogya 6.8.7 is read as 'sa ātmā atat tvam asi' ('you are not that'), taught nine times with examples to show difference (Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya 1).
summary: The Vedānta school founded by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), called by its adherents Tattvavāda, 'the doctrine of reality'. It teaches that Viṣṇu alone is the independent reality, that souls and matter are real, dependent and eternally distinct from him and from one another (the five differences), that souls are innately graded, and that liberation — the soul's enjoyment of its own bliss in Viṣṇu's presence — comes only by his grace, won through knowledge and devotion. Its classical literature runs from Madhva's thirty-seven works through Jayatīrtha's commentaries and Vyāsatīrtha's polemics to Rāghavendra; it is carried by ascetic maṭhas (the eight of Uḍupi with their biennial rotation of Kṛṣṇa worship, and the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) and was sung in Kannada by the Haridāsas.
notes: The tradition's teacher line before Madhva (the 'Haṃsa paramparā': Haṃsa-Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, the Sanaka group, Durvāsas, then a line of ascetics ending in Acyutaprekṣa) is recalled here only in outline; the intermediate names are not listed because they were not verified in this pass. A traditional verse likens the doctrine to a tree: seed sown by Vyāsa in the soil of śruti, sprouted by Madhva, branched by Jayatīrtha, leaved by Vyāsarāja, flowered by Vijayīndra and fruited by Rāghavendra (quoted as a preface verse in a modern edition in the raw_etexts corpus; author not identified). Further maṭhas (Śrīpādarāja maṭha at Mulbagal, Subrahmaṇya, Bhīmanakaṭṭe, Bhaṇḍārakeri; the Gauḍa Sārasvata Mādhva maṭhas of Kāśī and Gokarṇa-Partagāḷī) are mentioned without separate entries — details not verified.

name: Uttarādi Maṭha
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: One of the three principal Mādhva maṭhas (with the Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas). It traces its pontiffs from Madhva through Padmanābha Tīrtha, Narahari Tīrtha, Mādhava Tīrtha and Akṣobhya Tīrtha to Jayatīrtha and Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha; its later pontiffs include Raghūttama Tīrtha, Satyanātha Tīrtha and Satyadharma Tīrtha, most taking names beginning with 'Satya-'. It venerates Jayatīrtha's brindāvana at Malkheḍ.
notes: The division of the line after Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha (Kavīndra Tīrtha's line leading to this maṭha and, after a later split, to the Rāghavendra maṭha; Rājendra Tīrtha's line leading to the Vyāsarāja maṭha) is recorded here from memory at low confidence. The 'Mūla Rāma' images held by the tradition to have been brought from the Kaliṅga treasury by Narahari Tīrtha are claimed by this maṭha and the Rāghavendra maṭha — not verified.

name: Rāghavendra Maṭha (Mantrālaya)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha whose pontiffs included Surendra Tīrtha, Vijayīndra Tīrtha (Kumbhakonam), Sudhīndra Tīrtha and Rāghavendra Tīrtha; since Rāghavendra entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya on the Tuṅgabhadrā (1671) the seat and pilgrimage centre have been there.
notes: Its descent from Madhva via the Kavīndra Tīrtha line and a later division (Vibudhendra Tīrtha) is recorded at low confidence.

name: Vyāsarāja Maṭha (Sosale)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: The Mādhva maṭha of Vyāsatīrtha (Vyāsarāja), disciple of Brahmaṇya Tīrtha; seated at Sosale (Mysuru district). Vyāsatīrtha's brindāvana is at Nava Brindāvana near Ānegondi (Hampi).
notes: Its descent from Madhva through Rājendra Tīrtha, Jayadhvaja, Puruṣottama and Brahmaṇya Tīrtha is recorded from memory at low confidence.

name: The eight maṭhas of Uḍupi (aṣṭa-maṭha)
distinctive_positions: Shares the Dvaita doctrine of lin:dvaita without doctrinal difference; distinct as an institutional line of ascetic pontiffs (guru-paramparā), with its own images, brindāvanas and observances.
summary: Eight monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Madhva for eight of his ascetic disciples, who worship in turn the image of Kṛṣṇa that Madhva installed at Uḍupi: Palimaru (Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha), Adamaru (Narasiṃha Tīrtha), Krishnapura (Janārdana Tīrtha), Puttige (Upendra Tīrtha), Shirur (Vāmana Tīrtha), Sode (Viṣṇu Tīrtha, Madhva's brother), Kaniyooru (Rāma Tīrtha) and Pejavara (Adhokṣaja Tīrtha). The worship rotates among them (paryāya); the tradition credits Vādirāja Tīrtha of Sode with changing the turn from two months to two years (from 1522).
notes: The maṭhas are paired (Palimaru–Adamaru, Krishnapura–Puttige, Shirur–Sode, Kaniyooru–Pejavara) — recorded from memory, moderate confidence. The two-monthly original rotation and the 1522 date should be checked.
